scenes.name: Ice-T y el reality rap de Los Ángeles
scenes.book: The Come Up: An Oral History of the Rise of Hip-Hop
scenes.author: Jonathan Abrams
scenes.desc: Del electro de Radiotron, Ice-T (lector de Iceberg Slim, exmilitar, amigo de Afrika Islam, que lo llevó a Nueva York con Melle Mel y Caz) tomó de «P.S.K.» la entrega relajada: «6 ’N the Mornin’» (1986), cara B de «Dog ’N the Wax», con el 808 de Afrika Islam y DJ Unknown, contaba en primera persona la redada de las seis de la mañana, la cárcel, Crenshaw: bajó las pulsaciones del baile a la música para el coche de los lowriders. Rhyme Pays (Sire, 1987): Seymour Stein dudó y Ice le dijo «quizá eso que sientes es dinero»; nunca volvió a cuestionarle, ni con «Cop Killer». KDAY tuvo que retirarla por las quejas de C. Delores Tucker. Por la misma época, Toddy Tee vendía desde su coche «Batterram» (1985), sobre el ariete de la policía, y Mixmaster Spade era el dios de los buscavidas (Above the Law). Ice-T siempre contó las consecuencias: lo llamó reality rap.

xref.title: Early Label Rejection & Sire Signing (1975)
xref.body: The Ramones were signed by Seymour Stein to Sire Records in 1975 after he discovered them in a Manhattan bar. Other labels refused to sign them because they were considered "too weird," played "too fast," were "too amateurish," and "too funny looking." Mainstream rock radio also rejected them, seeing them as a joke. "back then, nobody wanted to touch the Ramones. They were just too weird. They played too fast. They were too amateurish. And they were too funny looking for all the other labels."

xref.title: Malcolm McLaren's Use of "New Wave"
xref.body: Malcolm McLaren, the manager of the Sex Pistols, frequently used the term "New Wave" in interviews. This contributed to Seymour Stein's consideration of the term for Sire Records' marketing campaign. "Malcolm McLaren, who was still the manager of the Sex Bistels at the time, peppered some of his interviews with this term."

xref.title: North American Importation by Seymour Stein
xref.body: The Smiths were one of several unknown English bands imported into North America by legendary record executive Seymour Stein, who was the founder of Sire Records. xref.title: Seymour Stein's Vision
xref.body: Seymour Stein, despite their unconventional sound, recognized the Ramones as a 60s-style pop band playing with the speed and volume of a jet engine. He loved their sound and was determined to sign them to Sire. "But Seymour, a guy who grew up on the music of the 50s and 60s, heard them for what they really were. A 60 style pop band that just happened to play their songs at the speed and volume of a jet engine."

xref.title: Sire Records Endorsement
xref.body: Seymour Stein, head of Sire Records, was drawn to The Pretenders, appreciating their edgy, punky sound, songwriting talent, and the image of a strong American woman (Chrissie Hynde) fronting a band that was 75% English, which he saw as the epitome of New Wave.
